body.text: There are good reasons to greet the P4M initiative with optimism. But if the group does not want to join the list of other well-intended, but failed initiatives to rescue multilateralism, it would be well-served to consider four action points

Amidst all the drama that surrounds the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, it is all too easy to miss out on some of the quiet and constructive work that happens on the sidelines. The Partners for Multilateralism (P4M), which was launched at the 81st UNGA Week in New York this September, could turn out to be one such initiative.

Co-sponsored by Australia, Brazil, Barbados, Canada, the European Union, India, and Kenya, and further signed by eighteen other countries, the P4M initiative commits to strengthening multilateral cooperation, and the institutions and rule of law that underpin it. This matters deeply at a time when multilateralism is under severe pressure. The United States - a principal founder and long-time guarantor of the system - is now rejecting it through word and deed; other major players are also flouting rules and norms with increasing frequency and impunity. Any declarations of support for multilateralism at this difficult time are only to be welcomed, and doubly so when they come from such a diverse group that includes large and small countries from the Global South and the Global North, and spans the world regions. Some of the language of the P4M declaration, moreover, is not status quo, but reform-oriented, for example: “we commit to strengthening multilateral cooperation that is open, fair, equitable, inclusive, networked and practical…”.

It is worth pointing out that from the perspective of the Global South, this reformist agenda is not a novel one. Developing countries have spent the last several decades seeking to make multilateral institutions “fair, equitable, inclusive”. But in the past, their critique had tended to produce patronising lectures on why the system worked, and advice that they just needed to get their own house in order to use the system effectively. Today, there is more of a receptive ear for the reform agenda in parts of the Global North. This is so for a variety of reasons, including political and economic turmoil within Western democracies and obvious weaknesses in the once unshakeable Transatlantic partnership, but also very much due to the growing clout of the Global South. P4M is interesting because it recognises and reflects the changing balance of power.
There are thus good reasons to greet the initiative with some optimism.
That said, if the group does not want to join the list of other well-intended, but failed initiatives to rescue and reform multilateralism, it would be well-served to focus on the following.
P4M needs to get cracking on a concrete plan of action, the costs of its implementation, and the distribution of these costs.

First, declarations can swiftly get consigned to the realm of “cheap talk” unless they are swiftly followed by clear, public indications of how their sponsors want to walk the talk. P4M needs to get cracking on a concrete plan of action, the costs of its implementation, and the distribution of these costs.

Second, to develop such a plan, the group needs to first establish clarity on the principles that will underpin its vision of an updated and reformed multilateralism. This, in turn, will require serious deliberation on how the group distinguishes itself from other endeavours, which also claim to support multilateralism, such as China’s four Global Initiatives.

Third, a problem with (otherwise) promising exercises to revamp the multilateral system is that they fail to engage with the affected populations. Even the best such efforts will attract the ire of the public if the global elite fail to communicate the relevance and expected impact of their systematically developed proposals. Multilateralism is an easy scapegoat to domestic populism at the best of times; at a time when global discontent is rife, it would be foolhardy to ignore the importance of public engagement and outreach by P4M members.

Finally, the P4M declaration makes the right noises about the need for multilateralism and the importance of reform. But it remains to be seen if it will be able to provide the necessary out-of-the-box thinking needed today to protect not just people, but also the planet. The diversity of its membership provides it with a potential treasure trove of alternative ideas on deep ecology and inter-species coexistence. A deep dive into these ideas with global thinkers and the P4M practitioners could develop an updated framework for multilateralism, which may have a chance to reduce the existential risks that affect us all.
This commentary originally appeared in The Indian Express.
